clinicalPearls: The end stage of a large, long-standing left-to-right shunt in which severe pulmonary vascular disease raises pulmonary resistance until the shunt reverses and becomes right-to-left, producing cyanosis
Arises from unrepaired defects with high pulmonary flow, such as large ventricular septal defects, atrial septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus, or complex lesions
Features central cyanosis, digital clubbing, and secondary erythrocytosis, with exertional breathlessness, fatigue, and reduced exercise tolerance
Multisystem complications include haemoptysis, paradoxical embolism and stroke, arrhythmia, hyperviscosity, gout, and bleeding tendencies
Systemic vasodilators are hazardous because they lower systemic vascular resistance and worsen right-to-left shunting and cyanosis, and must be avoided
Pregnancy carries very high maternal and fetal mortality and is strongly discouraged, with careful contraceptive counselling that avoids oestrogen-related thrombotic risk

Care is best delivered in specialist centres, focusing on avoiding destabilising factors, judicious use of pulmonary vasodilator (advanced) therapy, and consideration of transplantation in advanced disease
reference.pathophysiology: A large communication between the systemic and pulmonary circulations initially drives a high-volume left-to-right shunt. Sustained exposure of the pulmonary vasculature to high flow and pressure causes progressive remodelling with medial hypertrophy, intimal proliferation, and plexiform lesions, raising pulmonary vascular resistance irreversibly. When pulmonary resistance approaches or exceeds systemic resistance the shunt reverses, so deoxygenated blood enters the systemic circulation and causes cyanosis. Chronic hypoxaemia stimulates erythropoietin and secondary erythrocytosis, increasing viscosity, while the loss of the pulmonary filter allows paradoxical embolism; these mechanisms underlie the multisystem complications and explain why lowering systemic vascular resistance is dangerous.
additionalDifferentials: Cyanotic congenital heart disease without pulmonary vascular disease
Cor pulmonale from chronic lung disease
Pulmonary hypertension from left heart disease
Other causes of central cyanosis and clubbing
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography to identify the underlying defect, direction of shunting, and pulmonary pressures
Right heart catheterisation to measure pulmonary vascular resistance and assess reversibility
Pulse oximetry, including differential saturations, and full blood count for secondary erythrocytosis
Cardiac MRI or CT to define complex anatomy and detect pulmonary artery thrombus
Assessment for complications such as iron deficiency, hyperuricaemia, and renal impairment
redFlags: Worsening cyanosis or syncope indicating deteriorating haemodynamics
Massive or recurrent haemoptysis from pulmonary vascular disease
Pregnancy, which carries very high maternal mortality
Paradoxical embolism causing stroke or systemic embolism, and features of hyperviscosity
reference.prognosis: Eisenmenger syndrome shortens life expectancy but many patients survive into adulthood with specialist care; prognosis worsens with syncope, haemoptysis, right heart failure, and pregnancy, and transplantation is considered in advanced disease.
pitfalls: Prescribing systemic vasodilators that reduce systemic resistance and deepen right-to-left shunting
Routine venesection for erythrocytosis without hyperviscosity symptoms, which causes iron deficiency and paradoxically increases risk
Failing to counsel firmly against pregnancy and to advise safe, non-oestrogen contraception
Overlooking the risk of paradoxical embolism during intravenous access, requiring meticulous air-bubble precautions
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
ESC Guidelines for the management of adult congenital heart disease
management: Advanced pulmonary vasodilator therapy targeting the pulmonary vascular disease using endothelin receptor antagonists such as bosentan and phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors, with prostanoids in advanced disease
Avoidance of systemic vasodilators, abrupt volume depletion and other precipitants that lower systemic vascular resistance and worsen right-to-left shunting and cyanosis
Careful management of secondary erythrocytosis with attention to iron status and iron replacement for deficiency, reserving venesection for symptomatic hyperviscosity

Supportive care including symptom-directed supplemental oxygen, treatment of hyperuricaemia and gout, arrhythmia control and meticulous intravenous air-filter precautions to prevent paradoxical embolism
Surveillance with echocardiography, oximetry and full blood count for right heart failure, arrhythmia and haematological complications
Emergency management of haemoptysis, paradoxical embolism and stroke, and arrhythmia
Contraceptive counselling avoiding oestrogen-containing methods, with strong advice against pregnancy given very high maternal mortality
Referral to a specialist adult congenital heart disease and pulmonary hypertension centre, with consideration of heart-lung or lung transplantation in advanced disease
